---
pagetitle: "Steve Haigh · Computational Biology"
page-layout: custom
toc: false
lightbox: false
# The §01–§03 headers are structural, not linkable sections; anchor links would

anchor-sections: false
# Lets the homepage-only navbar rule live in styles.css beside the global one.
body-classes: nb-home
listing:
  - id: latest-post
    contents: blog/posts
    sort: "date desc"
    max-items: 1
    template: partials/latest-post.ejs
    date-format: "YYYY-MM-DD"
    fields: [date, title, description, categories, path]
include-in-header:
  - text: |
      <style>
        /* Homepage-only: the warm "paper" background for the showcase layout,
           and a full-width content area (the shared navbar supplies the header).
           The footer is hidden here — the page ends on its own easter-egg line.
           Scoped to index.qmd only. --nb-paper is redefined on body.quarto-dark
           in styles.css, so one rule covers both modes. The matching navbar
           rule lives in styles.css under body.nb-home, where it can be written
           to not collide with the global dark-navbar rule. */
        body { background: var(--nb-paper); }
        .nav-footer, footer.footer { display: none !important; }
        #quarto-content, main.content, .page-columns, .content {
          max-width: none !important;
          padding: 0 !important;
          margin: 0 !important;
          gap: 0 !important;
          grid-template-columns: none !important;
          display: block !important;
        }
      </style>

      <p class="nb-tagline">Computational biology, viewed from a 30-year software career.</p>
      <p class="nb-intro">Software developer of 30 years, now researching biomedical sciences at the University of Reading — extending the <em>wcEcoli</em> whole-cell framework to the first computational model of a human platelet.</p>

      <figure class="nb-fig nb-fig-tall">
        <a href="blog/posts/one-year-on/platelet-wcm-poster.pdf">
          <img src="blog/posts/one-year-on/platelet-wcm-poster.png" alt="Conference poster titled “Towards a whole-cell model of the human platelet” by Steve Haigh and Dr Mike Fry, School of Biological Sciences, University of Reading. Six sections explain why the platelet is the most tractable human cell to model whole (it has no nucleus, so no transcription or replication), how the wcEcoli bacterial framework was stripped back and rebuilt around the platelet calcium-release pathway, and how the model reproduces the measured calcium transient against published data. Figures show a schematic of the modelled systems, calcium and store traces before and after agonist, a dose-response surface over thrombin and ADP concentrations, and simulations of prostacyclin and clopidogrel. The stated conclusion is that the limit on a more complete model is the availability and consistency of quantitative data, not computation. The full text is in the linked PDF.">
        </a>
        <figcaption>Poster — Towards a whole-cell model of the human platelet. <span class="nb-figmeta">UK Platelet Society, Reading · Sep 2026 · click through for the PDF</span></figcaption>

Next up: finding a PhD, or funding to carry on with what I have started. In the meantime I am relearning the mathematics, plus a biochemistry course I started some time ago and intend to finish.</p>
